cheatSheet.title: Derivation of the Three Kinematic Equations
cheatSheet.summary: [IB MYP 4 • Sciences] Derivation of the Three Kinematic Equations: Exploring Orientation in space and time (scale, duration, and human journeys) through holistic criteria-based inquiry.
cueQuestions: How does Derivation of the Three Kinematic Equations model relationships and systems within Orientation in space and time?
How do we apply the core principles of Derivation of the Three Kinematic Equations to analyze experimental data under Criterion B & C?
What real-world ethical, environmental, and technological implications arise under Criterion D for Derivation of the Three Kinematic Equations?
cheatSheet.mainNotes:
**1. Foundational Concept & Global Inquiry (Criterion A & D)**:
• Core Definition: For motion under uniform (constant) acceleration along a straight line, kinematic parameters (initial velocity u, final velocity v, acceleration a, time t, and displacement s) are linked by three fundamental equations derived from velocity-time graph geometries.
• Global Context Focus: *Orientation in space and time (scale, duration, and human journeys)*.
• Key Governing Formula: $$v = u + at, \quad s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2, \quad v^2 = u^2 + 2as$$

**2. Investigation & Mathematical/Scientific Modeling (Criterion B & C)**:
• Key Observation: The kinematic equations apply ONLY when acceleration \(a\) is strictly constant.
• Dynamic Mechanism: Equation 1 \(v = u + at\) is derived directly from the slope of the v-t graph.
• Quantitative Relationship: Equation 2 \(s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2\) is the sum of the rectangular area \(u \cdot t\) and triangular area \(\frac{1}{2} (v-u) t\).

**3. IB Learner Profile & Conceptual Analogy**:
• Inquirer & Thinker: On a velocity-time graph, the slope represents acceleration, while the area underneath the line splits cleanly into a baseline rectangle (initial velocity x time) and an upper triangle (acceleration x time squared / 2).
• Real-World Inquiry: Automotive safety engineers calculate required braking distances and crumple zone collision times using kinematic formulas.

cheatSheet.title: Uniform Circular Motion & Centripetal Acceleration
cheatSheet.summary: [IB MYP 4 • Sciences] Uniform Circular Motion & Centripetal Acceleration: Exploring Identities and relationships (mental, physical, and ecological connections) through holistic criteria-based inquiry.
cueQuestions: How does Uniform Circular Motion & Centripetal Acceleration model relationships and systems within Identities and relationships?
How do we apply the core principles of Uniform Circular Motion & Centripetal Acceleration to analyze experimental data under Criterion B & C?
What real-world ethical, environmental, and technological implications arise under Criterion D for Uniform Circular Motion & Centripetal Acceleration?
cheatSheet.mainNotes:
**1. Foundational Concept & Global Inquiry (Criterion A & D)**:
• Core Definition: In uniform circular motion, an object moves along a circular path at constant speed, but experiences continuous inward acceleration (centripetal acceleration) due to the continuously changing direction of its velocity vector.
• Global Context Focus: *Identities and relationships (mental, physical, and ecological connections)*.
• Key Governing Formula: $$v = \frac{2\pi r}{T}, \quad a_c = \frac{v^2}{r} = \omega^2 r$$

**2. Investigation & Mathematical/Scientific Modeling (Criterion B & C)**:
• Key Observation: Uniform circular motion is an accelerated motion even though speed remains constant.
• Dynamic Mechanism: The linear velocity vector is always tangent to the circular trajectory at every point.
• Quantitative Relationship: Centripetal acceleration is directed perpendicularly to velocity, pointing radially inward toward the circle center.

**3. IB Learner Profile & Conceptual Analogy**:
• Inquirer & Thinker: Whirling a stone tied to a string: even if your hand turns at a perfectly constant rotational speed, the tension in the string must constantly pull inward toward your hand to prevent the stone from flying off along a tangent.
• Real-World Inquiry: Highway civil engineers bank circular curves on expressways so that the normal force component provides the necessary centripetal force without relying solely on tyre friction.
cheatSheet.coreAnalogy: IB Conceptual Intuition: Whirling a stone tied to a string: even if your hand turns at a perfectly constant rotational speed, the tension in the string must constantly pull inward toward your hand to prevent the stone from flying off along a tangent.
cheatSheet.curriculumTrap:
1. IB Assessment Pitfalls & Misconceptions:
1. **Confusing centripetal force with an outward fictitious "centrifugal force".**: Confusing centripetal force with an outward fictitious "centrifugal force".
   • **Remedy / Clarification**: In an inertial frame of reference, only the inward real centripetal force exists. If the constraint breaks, the body moves straight along the tangent, not radially outward.

2. Criterion Assessment Check:
• Criterion A (Knowing and Understanding): Explaining scientific knowledge to solve quantitative problems.
• Criterion B (Inquiring and Designing): Formulating testable hypotheses and designing reliable scientific investigations.

workedExample.problem: [IB MYP Criteria A & C Question • Level 7-8] A satellite orbits Earth in a circular path of radius \(7.0 \times 10^6\,\text{m}\) completing one orbit in 6000 seconds. Calculate its orbital speed and centripetal acceleration.
steps: Step 1 [Criterion A]: Speed \(v = \frac{2\pi r}{T} = \frac{2 \times 3.1416 \times 7.0 \times 10^6}{6000} = \frac{43.982 \times 10^6}{6000} \approx 7330\,\text{m/s}\).
Step 2 [Criterion B]: Centripetal acceleration \(a_c = \frac{v^2}{r} = \frac{(7330)^2}{7.0 \times 10^6} = \frac{5.373 \times 10^7}{7.0 \times 10^6} \approx 7.68\,\text{m/s}^2\).
workedExample.result: Solution: Orbital speed = 7330 m/s; Centripetal acceleration = 7.68 m/s² [Criterion A-C Level 8 Achievement]

cheatSheet.summary: [IB MYP 4 • Sciences] Newton's First Law: Inertia & Momentum: Exploring Fairness and development (resource sustainability and ethical responsibility) through holistic criteria-based inquiry.
cueQuestions: How does Newton's First Law: Inertia & Momentum model relationships and systems within Fairness and development?
How do we apply the core principles of Newton's First Law: Inertia & Momentum to analyze experimental data under Criterion B & C?
What real-world ethical, environmental, and technological implications arise under Criterion D for Newton's First Law: Inertia & Momentum?
cheatSheet.mainNotes:
**1. Foundational Concept & Global Inquiry (Criterion A & D)**:
• Core Definition: Newton's First Law (Law of Inertia) states that a body remains in its state of rest or uniform motion in a straight line unless acted upon by a non-zero net external unbalanced force. Mass is the quantitative measure of an object's inertia.
• Global Context Focus: *Fairness and development (resource sustainability and ethical responsibility)*.
• Key Governing Formula: $$\sum \vec{F} = 0 \implies \frac{d\vec{v}}{dt} = 0, \quad \vec{p} = m \vec{v}$$

**2. Investigation & Mathematical/Scientific Modeling (Criterion B & C)**:
• Key Observation: Inertia is an intrinsic property of mass: greater mass equals greater resistance to changes in state of motion.
• Dynamic Mechanism: Linear momentum \(p = mv\) quantifies the total quantity of motion contained within a moving mass.
• Quantitative Relationship: Forces do not cause motion; unbalanced net forces cause changes in motion (acceleration).

**3. IB Learner Profile & Conceptual Analogy**:
• Inquirer & Thinker: When a city bus brakes suddenly, standing passengers lurch forward not because an invisible force pushed them, but because their bodies possess inertia of motion and naturally continue moving at the bus’s previous speed.
• Real-World Inquiry: Automotive seatbelts and pre-tensioner airbags hold passengers firmly in place against inertia during rapid deceleration crashes.

1. IB Assessment Pitfalls & Misconceptions:
1. **Believing an object moving at constant velocity requires a continuous net driving force.**: Believing an object moving at constant velocity requires a continuous net driving force.
   • **Remedy / Clarification**: In the absence of friction and drag, zero net force is required to maintain infinite uniform velocity in a straight line.

2. Criterion Assessment Check:
• Criterion A (Knowing and Understanding): Explaining scientific knowledge to solve quantitative problems.
• Criterion B (Inquiring and Designing): Formulating testable hypotheses and designing reliable scientific investigations.

cheatSheet.title: Newton's Second Law: F = m*a
cheatSheet.summary: [IB MYP 4 • Sciences] Newton's Second Law: F = m*a: Exploring Globalization and sustainability (interconnected global cycles and human impact) through holistic criteria-based inquiry.
cueQuestions: How does Newton's Second Law: F = m*a model relationships and systems within Globalization and sustainability?
How do we apply the core principles of Newton's Second Law: F = m*a to analyze experimental data under Criterion B & C?
What real-world ethical, environmental, and technological implications arise under Criterion D for Newton's Second Law: F = m*a?
cheatSheet.mainNotes:
**1. Foundational Concept & Global Inquiry (Criterion A & D)**:
• Core Definition: Newton's Second Law states that the rate of change of linear momentum of an object is directly proportional to the applied unbalanced force and takes place in the direction of the force: \(F = \frac{dp}{dt} = m a\).
• Global Context Focus: *Globalization and sustainability (interconnected global cycles and human impact)*.
• Key Governing Formula: $$\vec{F}_{\text{net}} = \frac{\Delta \vec{p}}{\Delta t} = m \vec{a}, \quad \vec{J} = \vec{F}_{\text{net}} \Delta t = \Delta \vec{p}$$

**2. Investigation & Mathematical/Scientific Modeling (Criterion B & C)**:
• Key Observation: 1 Newton is the force required to accelerate a 1 kg mass at 1 m/s² (\(1\,\text{N} = 1\,\text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}^2\)).
• Dynamic Mechanism: Impulse \(J = F \Delta t = \Delta p\) is the change in momentum caused by a force acting over a duration.
• Quantitative Relationship: Acceleration is directly proportional to net force and inversely proportional to mass.

**3. IB Learner Profile & Conceptual Analogy**:
• Inquirer & Thinker: A cricket fielder draws their hands backward while catching a fast ball: increasing the impact time interval (\(\Delta t\)) drastically reduces the peak impact force (\(F = \Delta p / \Delta t\)) felt on the hands.
• Real-World Inquiry: Rocket propulsion engineers maximize thrust-to-weight ratios to produce immense upward acceleration during atmospheric ascent.
cheatSheet.coreAnalogy: IB Conceptual Intuition: A cricket fielder draws their hands backward while catching a fast ball: increasing the impact time interval (\(\Delta t\)) drastically reduces the peak impact force (\(F = \Delta p / \Delta t\)) felt on the hands.

1. IB Assessment Pitfalls & Misconceptions:
1. **Using total individual applied force instead of net unbalanced force in \(F = ma\).**: Using total individual applied force instead of net unbalanced force in \(F = ma\).
   • **Remedy / Clarification**: Always draw a free-body diagram and resolve \(\sum F = F_{\text{applied}} - F_{\text{friction}} = m a\).

2. Criterion Assessment Check:
• Criterion A (Knowing and Understanding): Explaining scientific knowledge to solve quantitative problems.
• Criterion B (Inquiring and Designing): Formulating testable hypotheses and designing reliable scientific investigations.

workedExample.problem: [IB MYP Criteria A & C Question • Level 7-8] A net force of 24 N acts on an 8 kg mass initially at rest for 5 seconds. Find: (a) acceleration, (b) final velocity, (c) total impulse delivered.
steps: Step 1 [Criterion A]: Acceleration \(a = \frac{F}{m} = \frac{24\,\text{N}}{8\,\text{kg}} = 3.0\,\text{m/s}^2\).
Step 2 [Criterion B]: Final velocity \(v = u + at = 0 + (3.0)(5) = 15.0\,\text{m/s}\).
Step 3 [Criterion C]: Impulse \(J = F \Delta t = 24 \times 5 = 120\,\text{N}\cdot\text{s}\) (or \(\Delta p = m(v - u) = 8 \times 15 = 120\,\text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}\)).
workedExample.result: Solution: a = 3.0 m/s²; v = 15.0 m/s; Impulse = 120 N·s [Criterion A-C Level 8 Achievement]

cheatSheet.title: Newton's Third Law & Momentum Conservation
cheatSheet.summary: [IB MYP 4 • Sciences] Newton's Third Law & Momentum Conservation: Exploring Scientific and technical innovation (exploring natural laws and systems) through holistic criteria-based inquiry.
cueQuestions: How does Newton's Third Law & Momentum Conservation model relationships and systems within Scientific and technical innovation?
How do we apply the core principles of Newton's Third Law & Momentum Conservation to analyze experimental data under Criterion B & C?
What real-world ethical, environmental, and technological implications arise under Criterion D for Newton's Third Law & Momentum Conservation?
cheatSheet.mainNotes:
**1. Foundational Concept & Global Inquiry (Criterion A & D)**:
• Core Definition: Newton’s Third Law states that for every action force, there is an equal and opposite reaction force acting simultaneously on different interacting bodies. In an isolated system with no external net force, total linear momentum is strictly conserved.
• Global Context Focus: *Scientific and technical innovation (exploring natural laws and systems)*.
• Key Governing Formula: $$\vec{F}_{AB} = -\vec{F}_{BA}, \quad m_1 u_1 + m_2 u_2 = m_1 v_1 + m_2 v_2$$

**2. Investigation & Mathematical/Scientific Modeling (Criterion B & C)**:
• Key Observation: Action and reaction forces never cancel each other out because they act on two entirely separate objects.
• Dynamic Mechanism: Action and reaction pairs are instantaneous, equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, and of identical physical nature.
• Quantitative Relationship: Law of Conservation of Linear Momentum follows directly from Newton’s Second and Third Laws.

**3. IB Learner Profile & Conceptual Analogy**:
• Inquirer & Thinker: Firing a cannon: the ignited gunpowder exerts a forward force on the cannonball, while the cannonball exerts an equal and opposite backward force on the cannon, causing it to recoil backward.
• Real-World Inquiry: Rocket engines eject high-velocity exhaust gases downward; the reaction force pushes the rocket upward into orbit in deep space.
cheatSheet.coreAnalogy: IB Conceptual Intuition: Firing a cannon: the ignited gunpowder exerts a forward force on the cannonball, while the cannonball exerts an equal and opposite backward force on the cannon, causing it to recoil backward.
cheatSheet.curriculumTrap:
1. IB Assessment Pitfalls & Misconceptions:
1. **Assuming normal force and gravitational force on a book resting on a table form an action-reaction pair.**: Assuming normal force and gravitational force on a book resting on a table form an action-reaction pair.
   • **Remedy / Clarification**: Both gravity and normal force act on the SAME book. The true reaction to Earth pulling the book down is the book pulling Earth up.

2. Criterion Assessment Check:
• Criterion A (Knowing and Understanding): Explaining scientific knowledge to solve quantitative problems.
• Criterion B (Inquiring and Designing): Formulating testable hypotheses and designing reliable scientific investigations.
cheatSheet.verificationProblem: IB MYP Inquiry Challenge: A 50 kg skater throws a 5 kg medicine ball horizontally at 6 m/s. What is the skater’s recoil speed on frictionless ice?

workedExample.problem: [IB MYP Criteria A & C Question • Level 7-8] A rifle of mass 4.0 kg fires a bullet of mass 0.02 kg with a muzzle velocity of 600 m/s. Calculate the recoil velocity of the rifle.
steps: Step 1 [Criterion A]: Total initial momentum before firing: \(p_i = (m_r + m_b)(0) = 0\).
Step 2 [Criterion B]: Apply momentum conservation: \(m_r v_r + m_b v_b = 0\).
Step 3 [Criterion C]: Substitute values: \(4.0 v_r + (0.02)(600) = 0 \implies 4.0 v_r + 12 = 0\).
Step 4 [Criterion A]: Recoil velocity: \(v_r = -\frac{12}{4.0} = -3.0\,\text{m/s}\) (the negative sign indicates motion opposite to the bullet).
workedExample.result: Solution: Recoil velocity = -3.0 m/s (3.0 m/s backwards) [Criterion A-C Level 8 Achievement]

cheatSheet.title: Universal Law of Gravitation (F = G*M*m/r²)
cheatSheet.summary: [IB MYP 4 • Sciences] Universal Law of Gravitation (F = G*M*m/r²): Exploring Orientation in space and time (scale, duration, and human journeys) through holistic criteria-based inquiry.
cueQuestions: How does Universal Law of Gravitation (F = G*M*m/r²) model relationships and systems within Orientation in space and time?
How do we apply the core principles of Universal Law of Gravitation (F = G*M*m/r²) to analyze experimental data under Criterion B & C?
What real-world ethical, environmental, and technological implications arise under Criterion D for Universal Law of Gravitation (F = G*M*m/r²)?
cheatSheet.mainNotes:
**1. Foundational Concept & Global Inquiry (Criterion A & D)**:
• Core Definition: Newton’s Universal Law of Gravitation states that every point mass attracts every other point mass with a force directly proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance separating their centers.
• Global Context Focus: *Orientation in space and time (scale, duration, and human journeys)*.
• Key Governing Formula: $$F = G \frac{M m}{r^2}, \quad G = 6.674 \times 10^{-11}\,\text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{kg}^2$$

**2. Investigation & Mathematical/Scientific Modeling (Criterion B & C)**:
• Key Observation: Gravitational constant \(G\) is a universal scalar constant, identical everywhere in the cosmos.
• Dynamic Mechanism: Gravity obeys an inverse-square law: \(F \propto \frac{1}{r^2}\).
• Quantitative Relationship: The gravitational force between everyday objects is extremely small due to the tiny magnitude of \(G\).

**3. IB Learner Profile & Conceptual Analogy**:
• Inquirer & Thinker: Gravity acts like an invisible universal tether between all matter: doubling the distance between two planets spreads the gravitational field over 4 times the spherical surface area, quartering the attractive pull.
• Real-World Inquiry: Astrophysicists use the universal law of gravitation to compute orbital trajectories for interplanetary spacecraft like Voyager and Artemis.
cheatSheet.coreAnalogy: IB Conceptual Intuition: Gravity acts like an invisible universal tether between all matter: doubling the distance between two planets spreads the gravitational field over 4 times the spherical surface area, quartering the attractive pull.
cheatSheet.curriculumTrap:
1. IB Assessment Pitfalls & Misconceptions:
1. **Confusing universal gravitational constant \(G\) with acceleration due to gravity \(g\).**: Confusing universal gravitational constant \(G\) with acceleration due to gravity \(g\).
   • **Remedy / Clarification**: \(G\) is a constant (\(6.674 \times 10^{-11}\)), whereas \(g\) is a local planetary acceleration (\(\approx 9.8\,\text{m/s}^2\) at Earth’s surface).

2. Criterion Assessment Check:
• Criterion A (Knowing and Understanding): Explaining scientific knowledge to solve quantitative problems.
• Criterion B (Inquiring and Designing): Formulating testable hypotheses and designing reliable scientific investigations.
cheatSheet.verificationProblem: IB MYP Inquiry Challenge: If the distance between two masses is tripled, by what factor does the gravitational force between them change?

workedExample.problem: [IB MYP Criteria A & C Question • Level 7-8] Calculate the gravitational attraction between Earth (\(M = 6.0 \times 10^{24}\,\text{kg}\)) and the Moon (\(m = 7.4 \times 10^{22}\,\text{kg}\)) separated by a center-to-center distance of \(3.84 \times 10^8\,\text{m}\).
steps: Step 1 [Criterion A]: Use \(F = G \frac{M m}{r^2}\).
Step 2 [Criterion B]: Numerator: \(6.674 \times 10^{-11} \times 6.0 \times 10^{24} \times 7.4 \times 10^{22} = 2.963 \times 10^{37}\).
Step 3 [Criterion C]: Denominator: \((3.84 \times 10^8)^2 = 1.4746 \times 10^{17}\).
Step 4 [Criterion A]: Force: \(F = \frac{2.963 \times 10^{37}}{1.4746 \times 10^{17}} \approx 2.01 \times 10^{20}\,\text{N}\).
workedExample.result: Solution: Gravitational force = 2.01 x 10^20 N [Criterion A-C Level 8 Achievement]

cheatSheet.title: Acceleration Due to Gravity (g) & Free Fall

cheatSheet.mainNotes:
**1. Foundational Concept & Global Inquiry (Criterion A & D)**:
• Core Definition: Free fall is the motion of an object subjected solely to gravitational force with zero air resistance. All objects, irrespective of their mass, fall near Earth’s surface with the identical acceleration \(g = \frac{GM}{R^2} \approx 9.8\,\text{m/s}^2\).
• Global Context Focus: *Identities and relationships (mental, physical, and ecological connections)*.
• Key Governing Formula: $$g = \frac{G M}{R^2}, \quad v = gt, \quad h = \frac{1}{2}gt^2, \quad v^2 = 2gh$$

**2. Investigation & Mathematical/Scientific Modeling (Criterion B & C)**:
• Key Observation: Acceleration due to gravity \(g\) is independent of the mass of the falling body.
• Dynamic Mechanism: Value of \(g\) is slightly higher at the poles than at the equator because Earth is an oblate spheroid (polar radius is smaller than equatorial radius).
• Quantitative Relationship: During upward vertical projection, acceleration is \(-g\); at maximum height, instantaneous velocity is zero.

**3. IB Learner Profile & Conceptual Analogy**:
• Inquirer & Thinker: In a vacuum chamber, a heavy bowling ball and an ultra-light bird feather dropped simultaneously strike the ground at the exact same millisecond because gravity accelerates every kilogram of mass at identical rates.
• Real-World Inquiry: Meteorologists and planetary scientists calculate atmospheric escape velocities and lunar gravity profiles using free fall physics.

steps: Step 1 [Criterion A]: Initial velocity \(u = 0\), height \(h = 44.1\,\text{m}\), \(g = 9.8\,\text{m/s}^2\).

cheatSheet.title: Mass vs Weight & Gravitational Potential
cheatSheet.summary: [IB MYP 4 • Sciences] Mass vs Weight & Gravitational Potential: Exploring Fairness and development (resource sustainability and ethical responsibility) through holistic criteria-based inquiry.

How do we apply the core principles of Mass vs Weight & Gravitational Potential to analyze experimental data under Criterion B & C?
What real-world ethical, environmental, and technological implications arise under Criterion D for Mass vs Weight & Gravitational Potential?
cheatSheet.mainNotes:
**1. Foundational Concept & Global Inquiry (Criterion A & D)**:
• Core Definition: Mass is the fundamental scalar measure of matter in a body that remains invariant across the universe, whereas weight is the downward gravitational force exerted on that mass by a celestial body (\(W = mg\)), varying with local gravity.
• Global Context Focus: *Fairness and development (resource sustainability and ethical responsibility)*.
• Key Governing Formula: $$W = m g, \quad g_{\text{moon}} = \frac{1}{6} g_{\text{earth}}$$

**2. Investigation & Mathematical/Scientific Modeling (Criterion B & C)**:
• Key Observation: Mass is measured in kilograms (kg) using a beam balance; weight is measured in Newtons (N) using a spring balance.
• Dynamic Mechanism: Weight is zero during free fall (apparent weightlessness in orbit).
• Quantitative Relationship: Weight changes with altitude above planetary surfaces and depth below Earth’s crust.

**3. IB Learner Profile & Conceptual Analogy**:
• Inquirer & Thinker: If you travel to the Moon, your body mass is still 60 kg (your cells and molecules have not disappeared), but bathroom scales show only 10 kg-force (98 N) because the Moon’s surface gravity is one-sixth of Earth’s.
• Real-World Inquiry: Spacecraft payload launch pricing is determined strictly by mass, but rocket booster thrust requirements are calculated against payload weight at liftoff.

cheatSheet.title: Scientific Work Done (W = F * d * cos θ)
cheatSheet.summary: [IB MYP 4 • Sciences] Scientific Work Done (W = F * d * cos θ): Exploring Globalization and sustainability (interconnected global cycles and human impact) through holistic criteria-based inquiry.
cueQuestions: How does Scientific Work Done (W = F * d * cos θ) model relationships and systems within Globalization and sustainability?
How do we apply the core principles of Scientific Work Done (W = F * d * cos θ) to analyze experimental data under Criterion B & C?
What real-world ethical, environmental, and technological implications arise under Criterion D for Scientific Work Done (W = F * d * cos θ)?
cheatSheet.mainNotes:
**1. Foundational Concept & Global Inquiry (Criterion A & D)**:
• Core Definition: In physics, mechanical work is done when an applied force causes a displacement along the line of action of the force. Work is a scalar quantity equal to the dot product of the force and displacement vectors: \(W = F d \cos \theta\).
• Global Context Focus: *Globalization and sustainability (interconnected global cycles and human impact)*.
• Key Governing Formula: $$W = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{d} = F d \cos \theta, \quad 1\,\text{Joule} = 1\,\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$$

**2. Investigation & Mathematical/Scientific Modeling (Criterion B & C)**:
• Key Observation: Positive Work: \(0^\circ \le \theta < 90^\circ\) (force aids motion, increasing energy).
• Dynamic Mechanism: Zero Work: \(\theta = 90^\circ\) (force perpendicular to motion, e.g. centripetal force).
• Quantitative Relationship: Negative Work: \(90^\circ < \theta \le 180^\circ\) (force opposes motion, e.g. kinetic friction).

**3. IB Learner Profile & Conceptual Analogy**:
• Inquirer & Thinker: Carrying a heavy suitcase while walking horizontally across a flat floor: despite your physical exhaustion, scientific work done by gravity is zero because the upward supporting force is perpendicular (90°) to horizontal displacement (\(\cos 90^\circ = 0\)).
• Real-World Inquiry: Hydraulic excavators and cranes calculate load hoisting capacity and electrical energy requirements via work-energy integral equations.
cheatSheet.coreAnalogy: IB Conceptual Intuition: Carrying a heavy suitcase while walking horizontally across a flat floor: despite your physical exhaustion, scientific work done by gravity is zero because the upward supporting force is perpendicular (90°) to horizontal displacement (\(\cos 90^\circ = 0\)).
cheatSheet.curriculumTrap:
1. IB Assessment Pitfalls & Misconceptions:
1. **Assuming work is done when pushing a rigid wall that does not move.**: Assuming work is done when pushing a rigid wall that does not move.
   • **Remedy / Clarification**: If displacement \(d = 0\), mechanical work \(W = 0\), regardless of how much physiological fatigue occurs.

2. Criterion Assessment Check:
• Criterion A (Knowing and Understanding): Explaining scientific knowledge to solve quantitative problems.
• Criterion B (Inquiring and Designing): Formulating testable hypotheses and designing reliable scientific investigations.

workedExample.problem: [IB MYP Criteria A & C Question • Level 7-8] A worker pulls a crate with a force of 150 N at an angle of 30° above the horizontal, moving it 8.0 m along the floor. Find the work done.
steps: Step 1 [Criterion A]: Identify values: \(F = 150\,\text{N}\), \(d = 8.0\,\text{m}\), \(\theta = 30^\circ\).
Step 2 [Criterion B]: Calculate work: \(W = F d \cos 30^\circ = 150 \times 8.0 \times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 1200 \times 0.8660 = 1039.2\,\text{J}\).
workedExample.result: Solution: Work done = 1039.2 Joules [Criterion A-C Level 8 Achievement]

cheatSheet.title: Kinetic Energy Derivation (KE = 1/2 m v²)
cheatSheet.summary: [IB MYP 4 • Sciences] Kinetic Energy Derivation (KE = 1/2 m v²): Exploring Scientific and technical innovation (exploring natural laws and systems) through holistic criteria-based inquiry.
cueQuestions: How does Kinetic Energy Derivation (KE = 1/2 m v²) model relationships and systems within Scientific and technical innovation?
How do we apply the core principles of Kinetic Energy Derivation (KE = 1/2 m v²) to analyze experimental data under Criterion B & C?
What real-world ethical, environmental, and technological implications arise under Criterion D for Kinetic Energy Derivation (KE = 1/2 m v²)?
cheatSheet.mainNotes:
**1. Foundational Concept & Global Inquiry (Criterion A & D)**:
• Core Definition: Kinetic energy is the mechanical work capacity possessed by a body due to its motion. Derived by integrating net work done to accelerate a body of mass \(m\) from rest to velocity \(v\): \(KE = \frac{1}{2} m v^2\). The Work-Energy Theorem states that net work done equals the change in kinetic energy.
• Global Context Focus: *Scientific and technical innovation (exploring natural laws and systems)*.
• Key Governing Formula: $$E_k = \frac{1}{2} m v^2, \quad W_{\text{net}} = \Delta E_k = \frac{1}{2} m v_f^2 - \frac{1}{2} m v_i^2$$

**2. Investigation & Mathematical/Scientific Modeling (Criterion B & C)**:
• Key Observation: Kinetic energy is proportional to mass \(m\) and to the square of velocity \(v^2\).
• Dynamic Mechanism: Kinetic energy is a scalar quantity and can never be negative.
• Quantitative Relationship: Work-Energy Theorem: \(W_{\text{net}} = \Delta KE\).

**3. IB Learner Profile & Conceptual Analogy**:
• Inquirer & Thinker: If you double the driving speed of a car from 30 km/h to 60 km/h, its kinetic energy quadruples (\(2^2 = 4\)), meaning brakes must do 4 times as much work and require 4 times the stopping distance.
• Real-World Inquiry: Crash barrier and runway runoff design engineers calculate stopping gravel bed depth based on aircraft maximum kinetic energy.

1. IB Assessment Pitfalls & Misconceptions:
1. **Assuming doubling speed doubles kinetic energy.**: Assuming doubling speed doubles kinetic energy.
   • **Remedy / Clarification**: Kinetic energy scales quadratically with speed: \(KE \propto v^2\). Tripling speed increases KE by a factor of 9.

2. Criterion Assessment Check:
• Criterion A (Knowing and Understanding): Explaining scientific knowledge to solve quantitative problems.
• Criterion B (Inquiring and Designing): Formulating testable hypotheses and designing reliable scientific investigations.
cheatSheet.verificationProblem: IB MYP Inquiry Challenge: What is the kinetic energy of an electron (mass = 9.1 x 10^-31 kg) moving at 2.0 x 10^6 m/s?

workedExample.problem: [IB MYP Criteria A & C Question • Level 7-8] A car of mass 1000 kg accelerates from 10 m/s to 25 m/s. Find the change in kinetic energy and net work done.
steps: Step 1 [Criterion A]: Initial KE: \(KE_i = \frac{1}{2}(1000)(10^2) = 500 \times 100 = 50,000\,\text{J} = 50\,\text{kJ}\).
Step 2 [Criterion B]: Final KE: \(KE_f = \frac{1}{2}(1000)(25^2) = 500 \times 625 = 312,500\,\text{J} = 312.5\,\text{kJ}\).
Step 3 [Criterion C]: Net Work: \(W_{\text{net}} = KE_f - KE_i = 312,500 - 50,000 = 262,500\,\text{J} = 262.5\,\text{kJ}\).
workedExample.result: Solution: Net work done = 262.5 kJ [Criterion A-C Level 8 Achievement]

cheatSheet.title: Gravitational Potential Energy & Energy Conservation
cheatSheet.summary: [IB MYP 4 • Sciences] Gravitational Potential Energy & Energy Conservation: Exploring Orientation in space and time (scale, duration, and human journeys) through holistic criteria-based inquiry.
cueQuestions: How does Gravitational Potential Energy & Energy Conservation model relationships and systems within Orientation in space and time?
How do we apply the core principles of Gravitational Potential Energy & Energy Conservation to analyze experimental data under Criterion B & C?
What real-world ethical, environmental, and technological implications arise under Criterion D for Gravitational Potential Energy & Energy Conservation?
cheatSheet.mainNotes:
**1. Foundational Concept & Global Inquiry (Criterion A & D)**:
• Core Definition: Gravitational Potential Energy (\(PE = mgh\)) is stored energy resulting from an object’s elevated position in a gravitational field. The Law of Conservation of Mechanical Energy states that in an isolated conservative system, total mechanical energy (\(E_{\text{total}} = KE + PE\)) remains strictly constant.
• Global Context Focus: *Orientation in space and time (scale, duration, and human journeys)*.
• Key Governing Formula: $$E_p = m g h, \quad E_{\text{mech}} = E_k + E_p = \text{constant}$$

**2. Investigation & Mathematical/Scientific Modeling (Criterion B & C)**:
• Key Observation: Gravitational potential energy is calculated relative to a chosen reference datum level (usually ground level \(h=0\)).
• Dynamic Mechanism: In free fall: \(\Delta PE_{\text{lost}} = \Delta KE_{\text{gained}}\).
• Quantitative Relationship: Power is the rate of doing work or transferring energy: \(P = \frac{W}{t} = \frac{\Delta E}{t}\) (Watts).

**3. IB Learner Profile & Conceptual Analogy**:
• Inquirer & Thinker: A roller coaster at the top of a peak has 100% potential energy and 0% kinetic energy. As it plunges down, potential energy transforms seamlessly into kinetic speed; at the lowest dip, kinetic energy is at its maximum while potential energy is at its minimum.
• Real-World Inquiry: Hydroelectric power plants harness gravitational potential energy from high-altitude reservoir water to spin turbines and generate electrical power.

cheatSheet.curriculumTrap:
1. IB Assessment Pitfalls & Misconceptions:
1. **Forgetting to include non-conservative dissipative forces like friction when applying total energy conservation.**: Forgetting to include non-conservative dissipative forces like friction when applying total energy conservation.
   • **Remedy / Clarification**: If friction is present: \(KE_i + PE_i = KE_f + PE_f + W_{\text{friction}}\).

2. Criterion Assessment Check:
• Criterion A (Knowing and Understanding): Explaining scientific knowledge to solve quantitative problems.
• Criterion B (Inquiring and Designing): Formulating testable hypotheses and designing reliable scientific investigations.
cheatSheet.verificationProblem: IB MYP Inquiry Challenge: A 0.5 kg ball is thrown vertically upward with 49 J of kinetic energy. What is the maximum height reached?

workedExample.problem: [IB MYP Criteria A & C Question • Level 7-8] A 2.0 kg pendulum bob is released from a height of 0.8 m above its lowest point. Find its velocity at the lowest point (neglecting air resistance, take g = 9.8 m/s²).
steps: Step 1 [Criterion A]: At release: \(KE_1 = 0\), \(PE_1 = mgh = (2.0)(9.8)(0.8) = 15.68\,\text{J}\).
Step 2 [Criterion B]: At lowest point: \(PE_2 = 0\), \(KE_2 = \frac{1}{2}mv^2\).
Step 3 [Criterion C]: Conservation of energy: \(KE_2 = PE_1 \implies \frac{1}{2}(2.0) v^2 = 15.68 \implies v^2 = 15.68 \implies v \approx 3.96\,\text{m/s}\).
workedExample.result: Solution: Velocity = 3.96 m/s [Criterion A-C Level 8 Achievement]

cheatSheet.title: Longitudinal Compression & Rarefaction Waves
cheatSheet.summary: [IB MYP 4 • Sciences] Longitudinal Compression & Rarefaction Waves: Exploring Identities and relationships (mental, physical, and ecological connections) through holistic criteria-based inquiry.
cueQuestions: How does Longitudinal Compression & Rarefaction Waves model relationships and systems within Identities and relationships?
How do we apply the core principles of Longitudinal Compression & Rarefaction Waves to analyze experimental data under Criterion B & C?
What real-world ethical, environmental, and technological implications arise under Criterion D for Longitudinal Compression & Rarefaction Waves?
cheatSheet.mainNotes:
**1. Foundational Concept & Global Inquiry (Criterion A & D)**:
• Core Definition: Sound is a mechanical longitudinal wave requiring a material medium for propagation. It propagates through sequential cycles of particle compression (high density and pressure) and rarefaction (low density and pressure) vibrating parallel to the direction of wave travel.
• Global Context Focus: *Identities and relationships (mental, physical, and ecological connections)*.
• Key Governing Formula: $$v = f \lambda = \frac{\lambda}{T}, \quad f = \frac{1}{T}$$

**2. Investigation & Mathematical/Scientific Modeling (Criterion B & C)**:
• Key Observation: Sound cannot propagate through a vacuum because it requires particle collisions.
• Dynamic Mechanism: Wavelength \(\lambda\) is the distance between two consecutive compressions or two consecutive rarefactions.
• Quantitative Relationship: Frequency \(f\) is the number of complete compression-rarefaction cycles per second (Hz).

**3. IB Learner Profile & Conceptual Analogy**:
• Inquirer & Thinker: Pushing and pulling the end of a stretched slinky spring: coils bunch together into dense traveling pulses (compressions) followed by spread-out loose regions (rarefactions) moving along the length of the spring.
• Real-World Inquiry: Acoustic architectural engineers design concert hall surfaces and diffusers to optimize wave compression phase relationships and eliminate dead spots.
cheatSheet.coreAnalogy: IB Conceptual Intuition: Pushing and pulling the end of a stretched slinky spring: coils bunch together into dense traveling pulses (compressions) followed by spread-out loose regions (rarefactions) moving along the length of the spring.
cheatSheet.curriculumTrap:
1. IB Assessment Pitfalls & Misconceptions:
1. **Confusing sound wave particle displacement with bulk medium flow.**: Confusing sound wave particle displacement with bulk medium flow.
   • **Remedy / Clarification**: Air particles do not travel from the speaker to the ear; they oscillate back and forth locally about their mean equilibrium positions, transferring acoustic energy.

2. Criterion Assessment Check:
• Criterion A (Knowing and Understanding): Explaining scientific knowledge to solve quantitative problems.
• Criterion B (Inquiring and Designing): Formulating testable hypotheses and designing reliable scientific investigations.

workedExample.problem: [IB MYP Criteria A & C Question • Level 7-8] A tuning fork produces a sound wave of frequency 512 Hz in air where the speed of sound is 340 m/s. Calculate its wavelength.
steps: Step 1 [Criterion A]: Use wave equation: \(v = f \lambda\).
Step 2 [Criterion B]: Rearrange for wavelength: \(\lambda = \frac{v}{f} = \frac{340\,\text{m/s}}{512\,\text{Hz}} \approx 0.664\,\text{m} = 66.4\,\text{cm}\).
workedExample.result: Solution: Wavelength = 0.664 m (66.4 cm) [Criterion A-C Level 8 Achievement]

cheatSheet.title: Speed of Sound Across Media Densities
cheatSheet.summary: [IB MYP 4 • Sciences] Speed of Sound Across Media Densities: Exploring Fairness and development (resource sustainability and ethical responsibility) through holistic criteria-based inquiry.
cueQuestions: How does Speed of Sound Across Media Densities model relationships and systems within Fairness and development?
How do we apply the core principles of Speed of Sound Across Media Densities to analyze experimental data under Criterion B & C?
What real-world ethical, environmental, and technological implications arise under Criterion D for Speed of Sound Across Media Densities?
cheatSheet.mainNotes:
**1. Foundational Concept & Global Inquiry (Criterion A & D)**:
• Core Definition: The speed of sound depends on the elasticity and density of the transmitting medium. Sound travels fastest through solids, slower through liquids, and slowest through gases (\(v_{\text{solid}} > v_{\text{liquid}} > v_{\text{gas}}\)) because tightly bound solid atomic lattices restore displaced particles much faster.
• Global Context Focus: *Fairness and development (resource sustainability and ethical responsibility)*.
• Key Governing Formula: $$v_{\text{sound}} = \sqrt{\frac{B}{\rho}} \quad \text{or} \quad v(T) = v_0 + 0.6\, T(^\circ\text{C})$$

**2. Investigation & Mathematical/Scientific Modeling (Criterion B & C)**:
• Key Observation: Speed of sound in dry air at 0°C is \(\approx 331\,\text{m/s}\); at 20°C it is \(\approx 343\,\text{m/s}\).
• Dynamic Mechanism: Speed of sound in fresh water is \(\approx 1480\,\text{m/s}\); in steel it is \(\approx 5960\,\text{m/s}\).
• Quantitative Relationship: Speed increases with increasing medium temperature and humidity in gases.

**3. IB Learner Profile & Conceptual Analogy**:
• Inquirer & Thinker: Passing a bucket of water down a human chain: if people stand shoulder-to-shoulder (dense, tightly bound solid lattice), the bucket travels down the line almost instantly compared to people spaced far apart (dilute gas particles).
• Real-World Inquiry: Geophysicists measure seismic P-waves (compressional acoustic waves) traveling through Earth’s crustal rock layers to locate earthquake epicenters.
cheatSheet.coreAnalogy: IB Conceptual Intuition: Passing a bucket of water down a human chain: if people stand shoulder-to-shoulder (dense, tightly bound solid lattice), the bucket travels down the line almost instantly compared to people spaced far apart (dilute gas particles).
cheatSheet.curriculumTrap:
1. IB Assessment Pitfalls & Misconceptions:
1. **Assuming sound travels fastest in gases because gas particles are free to move.**: Assuming sound travels fastest in gases because gas particles are free to move.
   • **Remedy / Clarification**: Sound speed is governed by elastic modulus over density. High lattice rigidity in solids transmits elastic stress waves far faster than gas collisions.

2. Criterion Assessment Check:
• Criterion A (Knowing and Understanding): Explaining scientific knowledge to solve quantitative problems.
• Criterion B (Inquiring and Designing): Formulating testable hypotheses and designing reliable scientific investigations.
cheatSheet.verificationProblem: IB MYP Inquiry Challenge: A sound wave travels through an iron rail (v = 5130 m/s) and through air (v = 340 m/s). Find the time difference if heard at a distance of 1.0 km.

workedExample.problem: [IB MYP Criteria A & C Question • Level 7-8] An observer sees a lightning flash and hears thunder 4.5 seconds later. If the air temperature is 20°C (speed of sound = 343 m/s), how far away was the lightning strike?
steps: Step 1 [Criterion A]: Speed of light is instantaneous (\(3 \times 10^8\,\text{m/s}\)) relative to sound.
Step 2 [Criterion B]: Distance \(d = v \times t = 343\,\text{m/s} \times 4.5\,\text{s} = 1543.5\,\text{m} \approx 1.54\,\text{km}\).
workedExample.result: Solution: Distance = 1.54 km [Criterion A-C Level 8 Achievement]

cheatSheet.realWorldUse: Geophysicists measure seismic P-waves (compressional acoustic waves) traveling through Earth’s crustal rock layers to locate earthquake epicenters.

cheatSheet.summary: [IB MYP 4 • Sciences] Echoes, Reverberation & SONAR Applications: Exploring Globalization and sustainability (interconnected global cycles and human impact) through holistic criteria-based inquiry.
cueQuestions: How does Echoes, Reverberation & SONAR Applications model relationships and systems within Globalization and sustainability?
How do we apply the core principles of Echoes, Reverberation & SONAR Applications to analyze experimental data under Criterion B & C?
What real-world ethical, environmental, and technological implications arise under Criterion D for Echoes, Reverberation & SONAR Applications?
cheatSheet.mainNotes:
**1. Foundational Concept & Global Inquiry (Criterion A & D)**:
• Core Definition: An echo is the distinct repetition of sound caused by reflection from an obstacle at a distance \(d \ge 17.2\,\text{m}\) (due to the 0.1 s human auditory persistence of hearing). SONAR (Sound Navigation and Ranging) utilizes high-frequency ultrasound pulses (> 20 kHz) to calculate oceanic depths and detect submerged obstacles via two-way travel time.
• Global Context Focus: *Globalization and sustainability (interconnected global cycles and human impact)*.
• Key Governing Formula: $$2d = v \cdot t \implies d = \frac{v \cdot t}{2}$$

cheatSheet.title: Kinetic Molecular Theory of Matter
cheatSheet.summary: [IB MYP 4 • Sciences] Kinetic Molecular Theory of Matter: Exploring Scientific and technical innovation (exploring natural laws and systems) through holistic criteria-based inquiry.
cueQuestions: How does Kinetic Molecular Theory of Matter model relationships and systems within Scientific and technical innovation?
How do we apply the core principles of Kinetic Molecular Theory of Matter to analyze experimental data under Criterion B & C?

cheatSheet.mainNotes:
**1. Foundational Concept & Global Inquiry (Criterion A & D)**:
• Core Definition: Matter consists of submicroscopic particles in continuous random motion. The average kinetic energy of these particles is directly proportional to absolute thermodynamic temperature in Kelvin.
• Global Context Focus: *Scientific and technical innovation (exploring natural laws and systems)*.
• Key Governing Formula: $$KE_{\text{avg}} = \frac{3}{2} k_B T, \quad T(\text{K}) = T(^\circ\text{C}) + 273.15$$

**2. Investigation & Mathematical/Scientific Modeling (Criterion B & C)**:
• Key Observation: Intermolecular forces are strongest in solids, intermediate in liquids, and negligible in ideal gases.
• Dynamic Mechanism: Kinetic energy is purely a function of absolute temperature (Kelvin).
• Quantitative Relationship: Diffusion rate increases with temperature and is inversely proportional to molecular mass (Graham’s Law).

**3. IB Learner Profile & Conceptual Analogy**:
• Inquirer & Thinker: Molecules behave like billiard balls bouncing on a vibrating pool table: increasing temperature speeds up table vibrations, causing balls to collide harder and push apart.
• Real-World Inquiry: Cryogenic preservation of stem cells relies on lowering temperature near 77 K to virtually halt molecular kinetic diffusion.

   • **Remedy / Clarification**: Temperature measures average kinetic energy per particle, whereas total heat depends on both temperature and particle count (mass).

2. Criterion Assessment Check:

cheatSheet.title: Latent Heat of Fusion & Vaporization
cheatSheet.summary: [IB MYP 4 • Sciences] Latent Heat of Fusion & Vaporization: Exploring Orientation in space and time (scale, duration, and human journeys) through holistic criteria-based inquiry.
cueQuestions: How does Latent Heat of Fusion & Vaporization model relationships and systems within Orientation in space and time?
How do we apply the core principles of Latent Heat of Fusion & Vaporization to analyze experimental data under Criterion B & C?
What real-world ethical, environmental, and technological implications arise under Criterion D for Latent Heat of Fusion & Vaporization?
cheatSheet.mainNotes:
**1. Foundational Concept & Global Inquiry (Criterion A & D)**:
• Core Definition: Latent heat is thermal energy absorbed or released during an isothermal phase transition (e.g. melting or boiling) to overcome intermolecular bonds without altering the temperature of the system.
• Global Context Focus: *Orientation in space and time (scale, duration, and human journeys)*.
• Key Governing Formula: $$Q = m L_f \quad \text{(Fusion)}, \quad Q = m L_v \quad \text{(Vaporization)}$$

**2. Investigation & Mathematical/Scientific Modeling (Criterion B & C)**:
• Key Observation: During phase transitions, temperature remains strictly constant despite continuous heat input.
• Dynamic Mechanism: Latent heat of vaporization for water (\(2.26 \times 10^6\,\text{J/kg}\)) is much higher than latent heat of fusion (\(3.34 \times 10^5\,\text{J/kg}\)) because boiling requires complete separation of hydrogen bonds.
• Quantitative Relationship: Steam burns at 100°C are much more severe than boiling water burns at 100°C due to released latent heat.

**3. IB Learner Profile & Conceptual Analogy**:
• Inquirer & Thinker: Unlocking heavy padlocks: energy is spent solely breaking chains between molecules rather than making them move faster, keeping the thermometer needle completely frozen at the phase transition temperature.
• Real-World Inquiry: Thermal storage systems in green buildings use phase change materials (PCMs) that absorb excess daytime heat via latent fusion.
cheatSheet.coreAnalogy: IB Conceptual Intuition: Unlocking heavy padlocks: energy is spent solely breaking chains between molecules rather than making them move faster, keeping the thermometer needle completely frozen at the phase transition temperature.
cheatSheet.curriculumTrap:
1. IB Assessment Pitfalls & Misconceptions:
1. **Using \(Q = m c \Delta T\) during a phase change.**: Using \(Q = m c \Delta T\) during a phase change.
   • **Remedy / Clarification**: During a phase change, \(\Delta T = 0\). You must use \(Q = m L\).

2. Criterion Assessment Check:
• Criterion A (Knowing and Understanding): Demonstrating knowledge of chemical principles and molecular behaviors.
• Criterion B (Inquiring and Designing): Designing safe chemical investigations with controlled variables.

workedExample.problem: [IB MYP Criteria A & C Question • Level 7-8] Calculate the total heat required to convert 0.5 kg of ice at 0°C into steam at 100°C. (Given: \(L_f = 3.34 \times 10^5\,\text{J/kg}\), \(c_w = 4186\,\text{J/(kg}\cdot\text{K)}\), \(L_v = 2.26 \times 10^6\,\text{J/kg}\)).
steps: Step 1 [Criterion A]: Step 1 (Melting): \(Q_1 = m L_f = 0.5 \times 3.34 \times 10^5 = 1.67 \times 10^5\,\text{J}\).
Step 2 [Criterion B]: Step 2 (Heating water 0°C to 100°C): \(Q_2 = m c \Delta T = 0.5 \times 4186 \times 100 = 2.093 \times 10^5\,\text{J}\).
Step 3 [Criterion C]: Step 3 (Vaporization): \(Q_3 = m L_v = 0.5 \times 2.26 \times 10^6 = 1.13 \times 10^6\,\text{J}\).
Step 4 [Criterion A]: Total Heat \(Q_{\text{total}} = Q_1 + Q_2 + Q_3 = 1.67\times 10^5 + 2.093\times 10^5 + 11.3\times 10^5 = 1.5063 \times 10^6\,\text{J} \approx 1.51\,\text{MJ}\).
workedExample.result: Solution: Total heat required = 1.51 MJ [Criterion A-C Level 8 Achievement]

cheatSheet.title: Evaporative Cooling Dynamics
cheatSheet.summary: [IB MYP 4 • Sciences] Evaporative Cooling Dynamics: Exploring Identities and relationships (mental, physical, and ecological connections) through holistic criteria-based inquiry.
cueQuestions: How does Evaporative Cooling Dynamics model relationships and systems within Identities and relationships?
How do we apply the core principles of Evaporative Cooling Dynamics to analyze experimental data under Criterion B & C?
What real-world ethical, environmental, and technological implications arise under Criterion D for Evaporative Cooling Dynamics?
cheatSheet.mainNotes:
**1. Foundational Concept & Global Inquiry (Criterion A & D)**:
• Core Definition: Evaporation is a surface phenomenon occurring at temperatures below the boiling point where high-kinetic-energy surface molecules escape into vapor, reducing the average kinetic energy and temperature of the remaining liquid.
• Global Context Focus: *Identities and relationships (mental, physical, and ecological connections)*.
• Key Governing Formula: $$\text{Evaporation Rate} \propto \frac{\text{Surface Area} \times \text{Temperature} \times \text{Wind Speed}}{\text{Humidity}}$$

**2. Investigation & Mathematical/Scientific Modeling (Criterion B & C)**:
• Key Observation: Evaporation occurs at any temperature on the liquid surface, unlike boiling which is a bulk phenomenon at a fixed boiling point.
• Dynamic Mechanism: Factors increasing evaporation: higher surface area, elevated temperature, higher wind velocity, and lower ambient humidity.
• Quantitative Relationship: Perspiration cools mammals through evaporative latent heat absorption from skin.

**3. IB Learner Profile & Conceptual Analogy**:
• Inquirer & Thinker: In a room of people where the fastest runners leave through an open exit door, the average running speed of the remaining crowd drops automatically.
• Real-World Inquiry: Industrial cooling towers in thermal power plants dump waste heat into the atmosphere using large-scale evaporative cooling.

1. **Confusing evaporation with boiling.**: Confusing evaporation with boiling.
   • **Remedy / Clarification**: Evaporation is a silent surface process below boiling point without bubbles; boiling is a bulk turbulent transition throughout the liquid volume at fixed boiling point.

2. Criterion Assessment Check:
• Criterion A (Knowing and Understanding): Demonstrating knowledge of chemical principles and molecular behaviors.
• Criterion B (Inquiring and Designing): Designing safe chemical investigations with controlled variables.

• Core Definition: Mixtures are classified based on dispersed particle diameters: True solutions (< 1 nm, homogeneous, transparent, stable), Colloids (1–1000 nm, heterogeneous, translucent, Tyndall positive), and Suspensions (> 1000 nm, heterogeneous, opaque, settle upon standing).

• Key Observation: True solutions pass through both filter paper and semi-permeable membranes without separation.
• Dynamic Mechanism: Colloids pass through filter paper but are retained by ultra-fine semipermeable membranes.

cheatSheet.title: The Tyndall Effect & Brownian Motion
cheatSheet.summary: [IB MYP 4 • Sciences] The Tyndall Effect & Brownian Motion: Exploring Globalization and sustainability (interconnected global cycles and human impact) through holistic criteria-based inquiry.
cueQuestions: How does The Tyndall Effect & Brownian Motion model relationships and systems within Globalization and sustainability?
How do we apply the core principles of The Tyndall Effect & Brownian Motion to analyze experimental data under Criterion B & C?
What real-world ethical, environmental, and technological implications arise under Criterion D for The Tyndall Effect & Brownian Motion?
cheatSheet.mainNotes:
**1. Foundational Concept & Global Inquiry (Criterion A & D)**:
• Core Definition: The Tyndall effect is the optical scattering of light by colloidal particles whose diameters are comparable to the wavelength of incident light, making the beam path visible. Brownian motion is the continuous zig-zag chaotic motion of colloidal particles caused by unequal collisions with solvent molecules, preventing gravity settling.
• Global Context Focus: *Globalization and sustainability (interconnected global cycles and human impact)*.
• Key Governing Formula: $$I_{\text{scattered}} \propto \frac{d^6}{\lambda^4}, \quad \bar{x}^2 = \frac{2 k_B T}{6 \pi \eta r} t$$

**2. Investigation & Mathematical/Scientific Modeling (Criterion B & C)**:
• Key Observation: True solutions do NOT exhibit Tyndall scattering because solute ions are too small (< 1 nm) to scatter visible light waves.
• Dynamic Mechanism: Brownian motion imparts mechanical stability to colloids by opposing downward gravitational sedimentation.
• Quantitative Relationship: Colloidal stability also stems from surface charge repulsion (zeta potential) across dispersed particles.

**3. IB Learner Profile & Conceptual Analogy**:
• Inquirer & Thinker: A beam of sunlight cutting through a dusty forest canopy or dark cinema hall illuminates tiny floating dust specks that dance continuously in random directions.
• Real-World Inquiry: Nephelometers in drinking water filtration plants use Tyndall light scattering to measure cloudiness and detect bacterial turbidity.

cheatSheet.title: Solution Concentration: Mass Percent & Molarity
cheatSheet.summary: [IB MYP 4 • Sciences] Solution Concentration: Mass Percent & Molarity: Exploring Scientific and technical innovation (exploring natural laws and systems) through holistic criteria-based inquiry.
cueQuestions: How does Solution Concentration: Mass Percent & Molarity model relationships and systems within Scientific and technical innovation?
How do we apply the core principles of Solution Concentration: Mass Percent & Molarity to analyze experimental data under Criterion B & C?
What real-world ethical, environmental, and technological implications arise under Criterion D for Solution Concentration: Mass Percent & Molarity?
cheatSheet.mainNotes:
**1. Foundational Concept & Global Inquiry (Criterion A & D)**:
• Core Definition: Solution concentration quantifies the relative amount of solute present in a given mass or volume of solution. Standard quantitative metrics include Mass Percentage (w/w%), Volume Percentage (v/v%), and Molarity (M, moles of solute per liter of solution).
• Global Context Focus: *Scientific and technical innovation (exploring natural laws and systems)*.
• Key Governing Formula: $$\text{Mass } \% = \frac{m_{\text{solute}}}{m_{\text{solution}}} \times 100, \quad M = \frac{n_{\text{solute}}}{V_{\text{solution (L)}}} = \frac{m}{M_r \cdot V}$$

**2. Investigation & Mathematical/Scientific Modeling (Criterion B & C)**:
• Key Observation: Mass of solution = Mass of solute + Mass of solvent (never forget to sum both in the denominator!).
• Dynamic Mechanism: Molarity is temperature-dependent because liquid volume expands with heating; mass percentage is temperature-independent.
• Quantitative Relationship: Dilution equation: \(M_1 V_1 = M_2 V_2\).

**3. IB Learner Profile & Conceptual Analogy**:
• Inquirer & Thinker: Adding concentrated syrup to milk: doubling syrup in the same glass doubles the sweetness (concentration), while adding more milk dilutes it without changing the absolute syrup quantity.
• Real-World Inquiry: Medical intravenous (IV) normal saline is formulated at precisely 0.9% w/v NaCl to remain isotonic with red blood cell cytoplasm.

cheatSheet.summary: [IB MYP 4 • Sciences] Laws of Chemical Combination (Mass & Proportions): Exploring Orientation in space and time (scale, duration, and human journeys) through holistic criteria-based inquiry.
cueQuestions: How does Laws of Chemical Combination (Mass & Proportions) model relationships and systems within Orientation in space and time?
How do we apply the core principles of Laws of Chemical Combination (Mass & Proportions) to analyze experimental data under Criterion B & C?
What real-world ethical, environmental, and technological implications arise under Criterion D for Laws of Chemical Combination (Mass & Proportions)?
cheatSheet.mainNotes:
**1. Foundational Concept & Global Inquiry (Criterion A & D)**:
• Core Definition: Chemical reactions obey the Law of Conservation of Mass (Lavoisier: mass cannot be created or destroyed in chemical transformations) and the Law of Definite Proportions (Proust: a pure chemical compound always contains elements in fixed, unvarying mass ratios regardless of origin).
• Global Context Focus: *Orientation in space and time (scale, duration, and human journeys)*.
• Key Governing Formula: $$\sum m_{\text{reactants}} = \sum m_{\text{products}}, \quad \text{Water } (H_2O) \implies m_H : m_O = 1 : 8$$

**2. Investigation & Mathematical/Scientific Modeling (Criterion B & C)**:
• Key Observation: Law of Conservation of Mass: \(m_{\text{total, before}} = m_{\text{total, after}}\) in non-nuclear reactions.
• Dynamic Mechanism: Law of Definite Proportions: Pure water whether from tap, river, or synthesis always possesses hydrogen and oxygen in a 1:8 mass ratio.
• Quantitative Relationship: Law of Multiple Proportions (Dalton): When two elements form multiple compounds, element mass ratios are small whole numbers (e.g. CO vs CO2).

**3. IB Learner Profile & Conceptual Analogy**:
• Inquirer & Thinker: Baking chocolate chip cookies: if you seal the ingredients in an airtight oven, the baked cookies weigh exactly the same as the raw dough, and every cookie contains ingredients in strict recipe proportions.
• Real-World Inquiry: Industrial synthetic ammonia plants (Haber-Bosch) use definite mass proportions to calculate exact nitrogen and hydrogen feedstock ratios.

workedExample.problem: [IB MYP Criteria A & C Question • Level 7-8] When 4.0 g of calcium carbonate is heated, it decomposes completely into 2.24 g of calcium oxide and carbon dioxide gas. Calculate the mass of CO2 evolved.
steps: Step 1 [Criterion A]: Reaction: \(\text{CaCO}_3(\text{s}) \rightarrow \text{CaO}(\text{s}) + \text{CO}_2(\text{g})\).

Step 3 [Criterion C]: \(4.00\,\text{g} = 2.24\,\text{g} + m_{\text{CO}_2}\).
Step 4 [Criterion A]: \(m_{\text{CO}_2} = 4.00 - 2.24 = 1.76\,\text{g}\).

cheatSheet.title: Dalton's Atomic Postulates & Modern Revisions
cheatSheet.summary: [IB MYP 4 • Sciences] Dalton's Atomic Postulates & Modern Revisions: Exploring Identities and relationships (mental, physical, and ecological connections) through holistic criteria-based inquiry.

cheatSheet.mainNotes:
**1. Foundational Concept & Global Inquiry (Criterion A & D)**:
• Core Definition: Dalton proposed that all matter is composed of indivisible, indestructible atoms. Modern atomic theory revised these postulates: atoms are divisible into subatomic particles (protons, neutrons, electrons), isotopes exist with different atomic masses, and mass-energy conversion occurs in nuclear reactions.
• Global Context Focus: *Identities and relationships (mental, physical, and ecological connections)*.
• Key Governing Formula: $$A = Z + N, \quad E = \Delta m \cdot c^2$$

**2. Investigation & Mathematical/Scientific Modeling (Criterion B & C)**:
• Key Observation: Dalton postulate: "Atoms are indivisible" -> Revised: Divisible into quarks, protons, neutrons, electrons.
• Dynamic Mechanism: Dalton postulate: "All atoms of an element are identical in mass" -> Revised: Isotopes (e.g., C-12 and C-14) have differing masses.
• Quantitative Relationship: Dalton postulate: "Atoms of different elements have different masses" -> Revised: Isobars (e.g., Ar-40 and Ca-40) share identical mass numbers.

**3. IB Learner Profile & Conceptual Analogy**:
• Inquirer & Thinker: Dalton viewed atoms like indivisible solid marble balls. Modern physics revealed atoms are like tiny solar systems containing an ultra-dense central nucleus surrounded by orbiting electron clouds.
• Real-World Inquiry: Carbon-14 radiocarbon dating uses atomic isotopic variations to determine archaeological artifact ages with high precision.

   • **Remedy / Clarification**: Dalton’s core concept that elements combine in small whole-number atomic ratios remains the absolute cornerstone of stoichiometry.

Step 2 [Criterion B]: Postulate 2: "Atoms are indivisible and indestructible." Revision: Discovery of radioactivity and nuclear fission proved atoms can split into subatomic particles and other elements.

cheatSheet.title: The Mole Concept & Avogadro's Number (N_A = 6.022e23)
cheatSheet.summary: [IB MYP 4 • Sciences] The Mole Concept & Avogadro's Number (N_A = 6.022e23): Exploring Fairness and development (resource sustainability and ethical responsibility) through holistic criteria-based inquiry.
cueQuestions: How does The Mole Concept & Avogadro's Number (N_A = 6.022e23) model relationships and systems within Fairness and development?
How do we apply the core principles of The Mole Concept & Avogadro's Number (N_A = 6.022e23) to analyze experimental data under Criterion B & C?
What real-world ethical, environmental, and technological implications arise under Criterion D for The Mole Concept & Avogadro's Number (N_A = 6.022e23)?
cheatSheet.mainNotes:
**1. Foundational Concept & Global Inquiry (Criterion A & D)**:
• Core Definition: One mole is the exact amount of substance containing \(6.02214076 \times 10^{23}\) elementary entities (Avogadro’s number \(N_A\)). The mass of one mole of a substance in grams is numerically equal to its relative formula mass.
• Global Context Focus: *Fairness and development (resource sustainability and ethical responsibility)*.
• Key Governing Formula: $$n = \frac{m}{M_r} = \frac{N}{N_A} = \frac{V_{\text{gas (STP)}}}{22.4\,\text{L}}$$

**2. Investigation & Mathematical/Scientific Modeling (Criterion B & C)**:
• Key Observation: Molar mass \(M_r\) is measured in grams per mole (g/mol).
• Dynamic Mechanism: At standard temperature and pressure (STP: 0°C, 1 atm), 1 mole of any ideal gas occupies \(22.4\,\text{L}\).
• Quantitative Relationship: 1 mole of \(H_2O\) contains \(6.022 \times 10^{23}\) molecules, \(1.204 \times 10^{24}\) hydrogen atoms, and \(6.022 \times 10^{23}\) oxygen atoms.

**3. IB Learner Profile & Conceptual Analogy**:
• Inquirer & Thinker: A "dozen" always means 12 items whether eggs or elephants; a "mole" always means \(6.022 \times 10^{23}\) chemical particles whether atoms, ions, or molecules.
• Real-World Inquiry: Chemical process engineers use mole balances to size industrial bioreactors and calculate exact stoichiometric reagent masses.
cheatSheet.coreAnalogy: IB Conceptual Intuition: A "dozen" always means 12 items whether eggs or elephants; a "mole" always means \(6.022 \times 10^{23}\) chemical particles whether atoms, ions, or molecules.
cheatSheet.curriculumTrap:
1. IB Assessment Pitfalls & Misconceptions:
1. **Confusing moles of molecules with moles of constituent atoms in polyatomic gases.**: Confusing moles of molecules with moles of constituent atoms in polyatomic gases.
   • **Remedy / Clarification**: 1 mole of oxygen gas (\(O_2\)) contains 1 mole of \(O_2\) molecules but 2 moles of \(O\) atoms (\(1.2044 \times 10^{24}\) atoms).

2. Criterion Assessment Check:
• Criterion A (Knowing and Understanding): Demonstrating knowledge of chemical principles and molecular behaviors.
• Criterion B (Inquiring and Designing): Designing safe chemical investigations with controlled variables.

workedExample.problem: [IB MYP Criteria A & C Question • Level 7-8] Calculate: (a) the number of moles in 88.0 g of \(\text{CO}_2\), (b) the total number of \(\text{CO}_2\) molecules, (c) total oxygen atoms present.
steps: Step 1 [Criterion A]: Molar mass of \(\text{CO}_2 = 12.01 + 2(16.00) = 44.01\,\text{g/mol}\).
Step 2 [Criterion B]: Moles \(n = \frac{m}{M} = \frac{88.0}{44.01} \approx 2.00\,\text{mol}\).
Step 3 [Criterion C]: Number of molecules \(N = n \times N_A = 2.00 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 1.2044 \times 10^{24}\) molecules.
Step 4 [Criterion A]: Each molecule has 2 oxygen atoms: total O atoms \(= 2 \times 1.2044 \times 10^{24} = 2.4088 \times 10^{24}\) atoms.
workedExample.result: Solution: 2.00 mol; 1.2044e24 molecules; 2.4088e24 O atoms [Criterion A-C Level 8 Achievement]

cheatSheet.title: Rutherford Gold Foil Experiment & Nucleus
cheatSheet.summary: [IB MYP 4 • Sciences] Rutherford Gold Foil Experiment & Nucleus: Exploring Globalization and sustainability (interconnected global cycles and human impact) through holistic criteria-based inquiry.
cueQuestions: How does Rutherford Gold Foil Experiment & Nucleus model relationships and systems within Globalization and sustainability?
How do we apply the core principles of Rutherford Gold Foil Experiment & Nucleus to analyze experimental data under Criterion B & C?
What real-world ethical, environmental, and technological implications arise under Criterion D for Rutherford Gold Foil Experiment & Nucleus?
cheatSheet.mainNotes:
**1. Foundational Concept & Global Inquiry (Criterion A & D)**:
• Core Definition: Rutherford bombarded ultra-thin gold foil with alpha particles: most passed undeflected, proving the atom is mostly empty space; rare large-angle deflections (> 90°) revealed that all positive charge and nearly all atomic mass is concentrated in a tiny central nucleus.
• Global Context Focus: *Globalization and sustainability (interconnected global cycles and human impact)*.
• Key Governing Formula: $$r_{\text{nucleus}} \approx 10^{-15}\,\text{m} \quad \text{vs} \quad r_{\text{atom}} \approx 10^{-10}\,\text{m}$$

**2. Investigation & Mathematical/Scientific Modeling (Criterion B & C)**:
• Key Observation: Over 99.9% of alpha particles passed straight through without deflection -> Atom is mostly hollow space.
• Dynamic Mechanism: A small fraction deflected at slight angles -> Positive charge is concentrated in a compact core (repelling positive alpha particles).
• Quantitative Relationship: About 1 in 20,000 bounced directly backward -> Nucleus is extremely small, rigid, and dense relative to total atomic volume.

**3. IB Learner Profile & Conceptual Analogy**:
• Inquirer & Thinker: Firing artillery shells at a piece of tissue paper: having a tiny fraction bounce straight back at you proved the tissue paper must contain tiny, ultra-dense steel ball bearings embedded inside.
• Real-World Inquiry: Rutherford Backscattering Spectrometry (RBS) is used in semiconductor fabrication to analyze the depth and composition of thin film layers.

1. **Assuming Rutherford’s model explained electron orbital stability.**: Assuming Rutherford’s model explained electron orbital stability.
   • **Remedy / Clarification**: According to classical Maxwell electrodynamics, accelerating orbiting electrons would continuously radiate energy and spiral into the nucleus in nanoseconds. This limitation was resolved by Bohr’s quantized model.

2. Criterion Assessment Check:
• Criterion A (Knowing and Understanding): Demonstrating knowledge of chemical principles and molecular behaviors.
• Criterion B (Inquiring and Designing): Designing safe chemical investigations with controlled variables.

cheatSheet.title: Bohr Atomic Model & Quantized Energy Shells
cheatSheet.summary: [IB MYP 4 • Sciences] Bohr Atomic Model & Quantized Energy Shells: Exploring Scientific and technical innovation (exploring natural laws and systems) through holistic criteria-based inquiry.
cueQuestions: How does Bohr Atomic Model & Quantized Energy Shells model relationships and systems within Scientific and technical innovation?
How do we apply the core principles of Bohr Atomic Model & Quantized Energy Shells to analyze experimental data under Criterion B & C?
What real-world ethical, environmental, and technological implications arise under Criterion D for Bohr Atomic Model & Quantized Energy Shells?
cheatSheet.mainNotes:
**1. Foundational Concept & Global Inquiry (Criterion A & D)**:
• Core Definition: Bohr resolved Rutherford’s stability dilemma by postulating that electrons orbit the nucleus only in discrete, non-radiating quantized energy levels (K, L, M, N shells with principal quantum numbers n = 1, 2, 3, 4). Radiation is emitted or absorbed only when electrons jump between energy levels.
• Global Context Focus: *Scientific and technical innovation (exploring natural laws and systems)*.
• Key Governing Formula: $$\Delta E = E_2 - E_1 = h \nu = \frac{h c}{\lambda}, \quad \text{Max electrons} = 2n^2$$

**2. Investigation & Mathematical/Scientific Modeling (Criterion B & C)**:
• Key Observation: Maximum electrons per shell given by \(2n^2\): K shell (n=1) = 2; L shell (n=2) = 8; M shell (n=3) = 18; N shell (n=4) = 32.
• Dynamic Mechanism: Electrons in stationary orbits do not lose energy by electromagnetic radiation.
• Quantitative Relationship: Valence shell cannot accommodate more than 8 electrons (Octet Rule).

**3. IB Learner Profile & Conceptual Analogy**:
• Inquirer & Thinker: Standing on a staircase ladder: you can stand stably on step 1 or step 2, but you cannot hover in the empty space between steps.
• Real-World Inquiry: Neon signs, street lighting, and flame spectroscopy rely on Bohr electron de-excitation emitting characteristic photon wavelengths.
cheatSheet.structuralRule: $$\Delta E = E_2 - E_1 = h \nu = \frac{h c}{\lambda}, \quad \text{Max electrons} = 2n^2$$
cheatSheet.coreAnalogy: IB Conceptual Intuition: Standing on a staircase ladder: you can stand stably on step 1 or step 2, but you cannot hover in the empty space between steps.
cheatSheet.curriculumTrap:
1. IB Assessment Pitfalls & Misconceptions:
1. **Filling M shell (n=3) with 18 electrons before placing any electrons in N shell (n=4).**: Filling M shell (n=3) with 18 electrons before placing any electrons in N shell (n=4).
   • **Remedy / Clarification**: In electronic configurations up to Calcium (Z=20), the outermost shell cannot exceed 8 electrons: Potassium (Z=19) is 2,8,8,1 (not 2,8,9).

2. Criterion Assessment Check:
• Criterion A (Knowing and Understanding): Demonstrating knowledge of chemical principles and molecular behaviors.

cheatSheet.title: Atomic Number, Mass Number, Isotopes & Isobars
cheatSheet.summary: [IB MYP 4 • Sciences] Atomic Number, Mass Number, Isotopes & Isobars: Exploring Orientation in space and time (scale, duration, and human journeys) through holistic criteria-based inquiry.
cueQuestions: How does Atomic Number, Mass Number, Isotopes & Isobars model relationships and systems within Orientation in space and time?

What real-world ethical, environmental, and technological implications arise under Criterion D for Atomic Number, Mass Number, Isotopes & Isobars?
cheatSheet.mainNotes:
**1. Foundational Concept & Global Inquiry (Criterion A & D)**:
• Core Definition: Atomic number (Z) is the number of protons defining element identity; Mass number (A) is total protons plus neutrons. Isotopes are atoms of the same element with identical Z but different neutron counts (and A); Isobars are atoms of different elements sharing identical mass number A.
• Global Context Focus: *Orientation in space and time (scale, duration, and human journeys)*.
• Key Governing Formula: $$A = Z + N, \quad A_{\text{avg}} = \sum (\text{Abundance}_i \times A_i)$$

**2. Investigation & Mathematical/Scientific Modeling (Criterion B & C)**:
• Key Observation: Isotopes possess identical chemical properties (same electron configuration) but differing physical properties (mass, density, radioactivity).
• Dynamic Mechanism: Chlorine-35 (75%) and Chlorine-37 (25%) give an average relative atomic mass of 35.5 u.
• Quantitative Relationship: Isobars (e.g. \(^{40}_{18}\text{Ar}\) and \(^{40}_{20}\text{Ca}\)) have different chemical properties despite equal mass numbers.

**3. IB Learner Profile & Conceptual Analogy**:
• Inquirer & Thinker: Identical twins (isotopes) share the same DNA/name (atomic number Z) but have slightly different body weights (mass number A) due to carrying extra backpacks (neutrons).
• Real-World Inquiry: Cobalt-60 isotopes are used in radiotherapy cancer treatment, while Carbon-14 is used in archaeological dating.
cheatSheet.coreAnalogy: IB Conceptual Intuition: Identical twins (isotopes) share the same DNA/name (atomic number Z) but have slightly different body weights (mass number A) due to carrying extra backpacks (neutrons).
cheatSheet.curriculumTrap:
1. IB Assessment Pitfalls & Misconceptions:
1. **Assuming isotopes of an element have different chemical reactions.**: Assuming isotopes of an element have different chemical reactions.
   • **Remedy / Clarification**: Chemical properties depend strictly on valence electrons (determined by Z). Isotopes have identical chemical reactivity.

2. Criterion Assessment Check:
• Criterion A (Knowing and Understanding): Demonstrating knowledge of chemical principles and molecular behaviors.
• Criterion B (Inquiring and Designing): Designing safe chemical investigations with controlled variables.

workedExample.problem: [IB MYP Criteria A & C Question • Level 7-8] Naturally occurring chlorine consists of 75% \(^{35}_{17}\text{Cl}\) and 25% \(^{37}_{17}\text{Cl}\). Calculate the average atomic mass of chlorine.
steps: Step 1 [Criterion A]: Average mass formula: \(A_{\text{avg}} = \frac{(75 \times 35) + (25 \times 37)}{100}\).
Step 2 [Criterion B]: Numerator: \(2625 + 925 = 3550\).
Step 3 [Criterion C]: Average mass: \(A_{\text{avg}} = \frac{3550}{100} = 35.5\,\text{u}\).
workedExample.result: Solution: Average atomic mass = 35.5 u [Criterion A-C Level 8 Achievement]

cheatSheet.title: Plasma Membrane & Osmotic Balances
cheatSheet.summary: [IB MYP 4 • Sciences] Plasma Membrane & Osmotic Balances: Exploring Identities and relationships (mental, physical, and ecological connections) through holistic criteria-based inquiry.
cueQuestions: How does Plasma Membrane & Osmotic Balances model relationships and systems within Identities and relationships?

What real-world ethical, environmental, and technological implications arise under Criterion D for Plasma Membrane & Osmotic Balances?
cheatSheet.mainNotes:
**1. Foundational Concept & Global Inquiry (Criterion A & D)**:
• Core Definition: The cell membrane is a selectively permeable phospholipid bilayer with embedded transport proteins that regulates the movement of substances. Osmosis is the passive net diffusion of water molecules across a semipermeable membrane down its water potential gradient.
• Global Context Focus: *Identities and relationships (mental, physical, and ecological connections)*.
• Key Governing Formula: $$\Psi = \Psi_s + \Psi_p, \quad \text{Hypotonic: Swell/Lysis}, \quad \text{Hypertonic: Plasmolysis}$$

**2. Investigation & Mathematical/Scientific Modeling (Criterion B & C)**:
• Key Observation: Hypotonic medium (higher water potential outside): water enters cell -> animal cells swell and lyse; plant cells become turgid.
• Dynamic Mechanism: Hypertonic medium (lower water potential outside): water exits cell -> animal cells crenate; plant cell protoplasts shrink away from wall (plasmolysis).
• Quantitative Relationship: Isotonic medium (equal water potential): zero net water flux, maintaining normal cell volume.

**3. IB Learner Profile & Conceptual Analogy**:
• Inquirer & Thinker: The plasma membrane is a gated security perimeter around a city: water slips freely through turnstiles (aquaporins), while ions and nutrients require authorized keycard gates (carrier proteins).
• Real-World Inquiry: Food preservation techniques (salting fish, making concentrated fruit jams) use hypertonic environments to plasmolyze and kill bacterial contaminants.
cheatSheet.coreAnalogy: IB Conceptual Intuition: The plasma membrane is a gated security perimeter around a city: water slips freely through turnstiles (aquaporins), while ions and nutrients require authorized keycard gates (carrier proteins).
cheatSheet.curriculumTrap:
1. IB Assessment Pitfalls & Misconceptions:
1. **Assuming water stops moving across the membrane in an isotonic solution.**: Assuming water stops moving across the membrane in an isotonic solution.
   • **Remedy / Clarification**: Water molecules continue moving across the membrane in dynamic equilibrium at equal rates in both directions (zero NET movement).

2. Criterion Assessment Check:
• Criterion A (Knowing and Understanding): Explaining biological mechanisms and cellular physiology.
• Criterion B (Inquiring and Designing): Planning controlled biological experiments and sampling methodologies.

workedExample.problem: [IB MYP Criteria A & C Question • Level 7-8] Describe what happens to: (a) a red blood cell, and (b) a leaf epidermal cell, when placed in a concentrated (hypertonic) salt solution.
steps: Step 1 [Criterion A]: (a) Red blood cell: Water moves out by exosmosis into the hypertonic solution; lacking a cell wall, the cell shrinks and crenates.
Step 2 [Criterion B]: (b) Plant cell: Water moves out of the central vacuole; the cytoplasm and plasma membrane shrink away from the rigid cellulose cell wall in a process called plasmolysis.
workedExample.result: Solution: RBC shrinks (crenation); Plant cell undergoes plasmolysis. [Criterion A-C Level 8 Achievement]
